FRAGMENTATION EVASION: Split probe packets into fragments too small for stateless inspection. --mtu X sets maximum transmission unit, forcing fragmentation. X must be multiple of 8. MECHANISM: TCP header is 20 bytes. With --mtu 8, header splits across 3 fragments. Stateless firewalls/IDS see only first fragment with source/dest IP but incomplete TCP header - may pass traffic. MODERN LIMITATION: Stateful firewalls reassemble before inspection. Most enterprise IDS (Suricata, Snort3) handle fragmentation. STILL WORKS AGAINST: Legacy firewalls, misconfigured iptables, some cloud ACLs, load balancers. DETECTION: Fragmented traffic on unusual ports is suspicious. Normal web traffic rarely fragments. --send-eth bypasses OS fragmentation for full control. ADVANCED: Combine with --data-length to pad fragments, --badsum to test if fragmented packets are checksummed.

MECHANISM: For each probe, nmap sends identical packets with different source IPs. Target sees scans from many IPs simultaneously. DEFENDER CHALLENGE: All decoys and real scanner look identical. NMAP DETECTION SIGNATURES: (1) SYN SCAN: High rate of SYN packets without completing handshake. Signature: >20 SYN to different ports from same source in 1 second. (2) NULL/FIN/XMAS: Illegal flag combinations. NULL = no flags, FIN only = no prior connection, XMAS = FIN+PSH+URG. Any of these = definite scan. (3) VERSION DETECTION: Banner grabs with unusual ordering. Nmap sends probes in specific sequence identifiable via timing pattern. (4) OS DETECTION: Malformed packets like TCP with undefined flag combinations, ICMP with unusual payloads, IP options rarely used in legitimate traffic. (5) NSE SCRIPTS: Script-specific patterns like SMB null session attempts, HTTP requests to non-existent paths. SNORT RULES: 'alert tcp any any -> any any (flags:S; threshold: type threshold, track by_src, count 20, seconds 1; msg:"Possible SYN scan"; sid:1000001;)'. SURICATA: Built-in scan detection in suricata.yaml -> detect-engine -> rule-profiling.

chunks.content: NMAP LEAVES FINGERPRINTS: Even careful attackers can be identified as using nmap. DETECTION VECTORS: (1) TCP OPTIONS ORDER: Nmap uses MSS,SACK,TS,NOP,WS in specific order, different from OS stacks. (2) WINDOW SIZE: Nmap SYN probes use window size 1024 (common), but OS detection probes use specific values like 65535, 512, etc. rarely seen naturally. (3) TTL VALUES: Nmap defaults may differ from host OS. Linux nmap on Linux sends TTL 64, but scan packets may have TTL 37-64 from probes. (4) TIMING PATTERNS: Script engine has characteristic pause patterns between probe types. (5) USER-AGENT: http-* scripts use 'Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; Nmap Scripting Engine; https://nmap.org/book/nse.html)' unless changed. (6) PROBE SEQUENCES: Version detection sends probes in documented order. COUNTERMEASURE: p0f tool passively fingerprints remote OS including scanner tools. Zeek/Bro logs TCP options for analysis. EVASION: --data-length, --ttl, --spoof-mac change some signatures but not all.

LAYERED DEFENSE: (1) PERIMETER: Rate-limit new connections per source IP. iptables: -m recent --update --seconds 60 --hitcount 20 -j DROP. Blocks rapid port scanning. (2) HOST FIREWALL: Default deny inbound. Only allow required ports from authorized sources. (3) PORT KNOCKING: Require specific sequence before port opens. Invisible to scanners. (4) TAR PIT: Slow down attackers with delayed responses. LaBrea, iptables TARPIT target. Wastes scanner time. (5) DECEPTION: Honeypots return fake open ports. Portspoof returns fake banners for all 65535 ports, making scans useless. (6) LOGGING: Log all SYN packets for forensics. iptables -j LOG --log-prefix 'SYN: '. (7) BEHAVIORAL: Fail2ban/CrowdSec auto-block IPs exceeding thresholds. NETWORK: Implement BCP38 (anti-spoofing) to prevent idle scans using your network. CLOUD: AWS Security Groups, Azure NSG - default deny, log with VPC Flow Logs.

COMMON MISCONCEPTION: 'Host not responding? Use -Pn!' REALITY: -Pn skips host discovery, assuming ALL hosts are up. LOAD BALANCER CHALLENGES: (1) Different backend servers have different services. Scan shows union of all backends. (2) Stateless scanning hits different backends per probe - inconsistent results. (3) Health checks may open ports that backends don't serve. (4) Source IP persistence means retries hit same backend - incomplete picture. NAT CHALLENGES: (1) Port forwarding maps external port to different internal port - version detection may be wrong service. (2) Many internal hosts behind one IP - can't enumerate all. (3) Connection tracking affects scan behavior - RST from NAT vs host. DETECTION: Inconsistent banners on same port = load balancer. TTL variations = multiple backends. TECHNIQUES: Run scan multiple times and diff results. Use --max-retries 0 to minimize backend affinity. Add -sV with high intensity to get more banners per backend.

chunks.content: ASYMMETRIC ROUTING: Packets take different paths to and from target. PROBLEMS: (1) Your scan reaches target via path A, response returns via path B. IDLE SCAN PRINCIPLE: Infer target port state by observing IP ID changes on a 'zombie' host, without sending packets from your IP to target. IP ID is a 16-bit field in IPv4 header used for fragment reassembly. ZOMBIE REQUIREMENT: Must have GLOBALLY INCREMENTING IP ID - each packet the zombie sends increments its IP ID by exactly 1. WHY: (1) You send SYN to TARGET with SPOOFED source = zombie IP, (2) If port OPEN: target sends SYN-ACK to zombie, zombie sends RST (incrementing its IP ID), (3) If port CLOSED: target sends RST to zombie, zombie ignores it (no increment), (4) You probe zombie's IP ID before and after - if it increased by 2 instead of 1, port was open. MODERN CHALLENGE: Most modern OS randomize IP ID per-connection (Linux 4.1+, Windows 10+, BSD). GOOD ZOMBIES: Old printers, IoT devices, legacy Windows (XP/2003), embedded systems. TEST ZOMBIE: nmap -O -v zombie_ip - look for 'IP ID Sequence: Incremental' in output.

chunks.content: IPv6 SCANNING CHALLENGES: (1) Address space is 2^128 - brute force host discovery impossible. A /64 subnet has 18 quintillion addresses. (2) No ARP - uses ICMPv6 Neighbor Discovery instead. (3) Multiple addresses per host (link-local fe80::, global, temporary privacy addresses). (4) Many networks are dual-stack - scan both protocols. DISCOVERY TECHNIQUES: (1) Multicast ping: ping6 ff02::1%eth0 reaches all link-local nodes. (2) DNS enumeration: AAAA records reveal IPv6 addresses. (3) IPv4 mapping: Convert known IPv4 hosts to IPv6 (stateless addressing uses MAC). (4) Traffic sniffing: Passive discovery of active IPv6 hosts. NMAP IPv6: Use -6 flag. Host discovery uses ICMPv6 echo, TCP SYN, UDP. Many firewalls neglect IPv6 rules - potential bypass. COMMON PATTERNS: ::1 (localhost), fe80::/10 (link-local), 2000::/3 (global unicast), ff00::/8 (multicast).

Equivalent to TCP SYN scan. -sZ (SCTP COOKIE-ECHO scan): More stealthy, sends COOKIE-ECHO which is dropped by open ports (no state), ABORT from closed. CRITICAL: SOCKS proxies operate at OSI Layer 5 (session layer) and can ONLY proxy established TCP connections, NOT raw IP packets. This is why -sS (SYN scan) FAILS through SOCKS: (1) SYN scans require CAP_NET_RAW to craft custom TCP headers with only SYN flag set, (2) SOCKS protocol has no mechanism to encapsulate arbitrary IP packets - it only understands CONNECT requests for TCP streams, (3) When nmap sends a raw SYN packet, the local kernel has no route through the SOCKS proxy. SOLUTION: Use -sT (TCP connect scan) which uses the OS connect() syscall to establish full TCP connections. The kernel routes these through proxychains normally. TRADE-OFFS: -sT is slower (full 3-way handshake vs half-open), more detectable (connection fully established), and leaves logs on target (accept() called). ALSO INCOMPATIBLE: -sU (UDP), -sA (ACK), -sW (Window), -sM (Maimon), -sN/-sF/-sX (NULL/FIN/Xmas) - ALL require raw sockets.

chunks.content: THREE MAIN PIVOT METHODS: (1) SSH SOCKS Proxy (-D): Creates SOCKS4a/5 proxy on local port, requires proxychains, only TCP connect scans work, simple to set up. Command: ssh -D 9050 user@pivot. (2) SSH Local Port Forward (-L): Forwards specific local port to remote host:port, no proxychains needed, nmap connects directly to localhost:port, but only ONE target port at a time. Command: ssh -L 8445:internal:445 user@pivot then nmap -sT -p 8445 localhost. (3) VPN/Tun (sshuttle, OpenVPN, WireGuard): Creates Layer 3 tunnel, ALL scan types work including -sS/-sU, nmap sees real internal IPs, most transparent but requires root on pivot or VPN server. COMPARISON: SOCKS is easiest but most limited. Local forward is surgical but tedious for many ports. VPN is most powerful but hardest to set up in pentest scenarios. EXPERT TIP: Use sshuttle for quick Layer 3 tunnel without full VPN: sshuttle -r user@pivot 10.0.0.0/8 --dns

chunks.content: MULTI-HOP REALITY: Each pivot adds 50-200ms latency. A double-pivot (you -> DMZ -> internal -> target) means 100-400ms round-trip MINIMUM. Nmap default timeouts assume <100ms latency. CRITICAL ADJUSTMENTS: (1) Increase --host-timeout to 30m or higher, (2) Use --max-retries 3 or higher, (3) Set --min-rtt-timeout 500ms and --max-rtt-timeout 5s, (4) Reduce parallelism with --max-parallelism 5 to prevent proxy overload. PROXYCHAINS CHAINING: Edit /etc/proxychains.conf with multiple SOCKS proxies in order - traffic flows through each sequentially. Use 'strict_chain' mode for predictable routing. DOUBLE SSH: ssh -J user@hop1 user@hop2 -D 9050 creates SOCKS through two SSH hops. LATENCY KILL: A /24 subnet scan that takes 5 minutes direct can take 2+ HOURS through double pivot. Prioritize port selection ruthlessly.

Use Case: Scanning through double pivot without timeouts

TIMING AS FINGERPRINT: Beyond version strings, response timing reveals implementation details. TECHNIQUES: (1) TCP handshake timing: Time between SYN and SYN-ACK varies by OS/implementation. Linux ~0.5ms local, Windows ~1-2ms. (2) Application response timing: Database query time reveals backend. Instant response = cached, 100ms+ = disk query, 500ms+ = complex join. (3) Error handling timing: Invalid input processed faster than valid-but-wrong = indicates input validation logic. (4) Crypto timing: Weak implementations leak key bits through decrypt time. NMAP TIMING: Use --min-rtt-timeout and --initial-rtt-timeout to measure baseline. Script timing: capture output with timestamps. ADVANCED: Use hping3 for microsecond precision TCP timing. DEFENSE EVASION: Consistent timing = protection. Add random delays to mask processing time.
